| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Uptime       | Requests a URL and checks the status            | Full outages, DNS faults, expired certificates |
| API          | Calls endpoints in sequence, validates replies  | Broken contracts and authentication      |
| Browser      | Drives a real browser through a user journey    | Broken pages and script errors           |
| Multi-region | Runs the same check from several locations      | Regional routing failures                |

The main use is covering quiet periods. A bad deployment at 3am breaks login, no customers are awake to notice, and the first report arrives at 8am. A scripted login every minute would have raised an [alert](node:Alert) within minutes, which directly lowers [MTTD](node:MTTD).

The limits come from the fact that the users are not real. Only the scripted paths are covered. A clean browser on a fast datacenter connection does not represent an old phone on a slow network, so pair it with [real user monitoring](node:Real%20user%20monitoring).

A few practices keep checks trustworthy. Require failures from more than one location before paging, so that a network problem at one probe does not wake anyone. Use dedicated test accounts and tag the traffic so it stays out of business analytics and any [SLI](node:SLI) based on real users. Avoid real side effects such as live payments. Maintain the scripts, because a redesigned button will fail a browser check, and a check that fails routinely contributes to [alert fatigue](node:Alert%20fatigue).
quotes: Nobody noticed the password reset was broken until Monday.
It gets almost no weekend traffic. Add a synthetic monitoring check for that flow so we don't rely on users reporting it.

nodes.name: Real user monitoring
nodes.description: Collecting performance and error data from actual users' browsers or apps as they use the product.
nodes.markdown:
Real user [monitoring](node:Monitoring) (RUM) is collecting performance and error data from real users' browsers or apps during real sessions. A small script or SDK measures page loads, interactions and client-side errors, then sends the results to a backend.

It is usually paired with [synthetic monitoring](node:Synthetic%20monitoring), and the two have opposite strengths:

| Aspect                | Real user monitoring                 | Synthetic monitoring              |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------- |
| Traffic               | Real users                           | Scripted checks                   |
| Coverage              | The devices and networks users have  | Chosen paths and locations        |
| Works with no traffic | No                                   | Yes                               |
| Stable over time      | Noisy, as the user mix changes       | Stable baseline                   |
| Good at finding       | Problems affecting one segment       | Outages on known paths            |

RUM shows what server-side [metrics](node:Metric) cannot. A server can report an 80 ms response while the user waits six seconds, because the time went to the network, a large script bundle or page rendering. The familiar symptom is a backend dashboard that looks fine while users in one country on mobile complain. Segmenting by device, browser, country, connection type and release version usually exposes the group affected. Use [percentiles](node:Percentile), because client timings have a long tail.

RUM has a blind spot during severe failures. If a page fails to load at all, its script may never run, so the outage appears as a drop in sessions and not as a rise in errors. Ad blockers and privacy settings also block some reporting. Watch session volume alongside error rate.

Because RUM runs on users' devices, privacy needs attention. URLs and form fields can contain personal data, and session recording can capture more. Collect the minimum, mask sensitive fields and follow consent rules. The script itself adds page weight, so keep it small.
quotes: Our API p95 is 90 ms, so I don't buy that the app feels slow.
Real user monitoring says p75 load on Android in Brazil is nine seconds. The API isn't where that time is going.

nodes.name: Alert
nodes.description: An automated notification that a monitored condition has been met and may need someone's attention.
nodes.markdown:
An alert is an automated notification that a monitored condition has been met. It is defined by a rule such as "error rate above 2% for 5 minutes", a severity, a destination and ideally a link to a [runbook](node:Runbook). The duration in the rule filters out brief blips, at the price of a slower response.

Alerts should be routed according to how quickly someone needs to act:

| Level     | Delivery                  | Expected response           | Example                    |
| --------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Page      | Phone call or push        | Act within minutes          | Checkout is failing        |
| Ticket    | Issue queue               | Act within days             | Disk fills in two weeks    |
| Record    | Dashboard, no notification | Read during investigation  | Brief spike in retries     |

The test for a page is whether a person needs to do something now. A page that wakes an engineer for a condition that clears itself before they have opened a laptop teaches them to ignore the next one, which leads to [alert fatigue](node:Alert%20fatigue). If no action is needed, make it a ticket or remove it.

Flapping is a common defect, where a value hovers around the threshold and the alert fires and clears repeatedly. Use a longer window, or separate thresholds for firing and clearing.

A useful page says what is broken and who is affected. "HighCPU on host-17" leaves the responder to work out whether anything matters. "Checkout error rate 4%, EU users affected" with links to a dashboard and runbook gives a starting point.

Grouping related alerts stops one outage from sending 200 notifications. Silences for planned maintenance should have an expiry.

Pages are generally tied to user impact through [symptom-based alerting](node:Symptom-based%20alerting), often as a [burn rate alert](node:Burn%20rate%20alert) on an [SLO](node:SLO). They go to whoever is [on-call](node:On-call).
quotes: I got paged for high memory at 4am and it was gone by the time I logged in.
Then that alert shouldn't page. Downgrade it to a ticket and page on user-facing errors instead.

nodes.name: Alert fatigue
nodes.description: When frequent or low-value alerts train responders to ignore them, so real problems get missed or handled late.
nodes.markdown:
[Alert](node:Alert) fatigue is the loss of attention that happens when responders receive so many low-value alerts that they stop treating each one as meaningful. In practice, the phone goes off, the [on-call](node:On-call) engineer acknowledges it without reading because it is usually nothing, and the one page that mattered looks the same as the forty that did not.

Each cause has a specific fix:

| Cause               | Example                             | Fix                                       |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Not actionable      | CPU high with no user impact        | Remove it or make it a ticket             |
| Threshold too tight | Fires at every daily traffic peak   | Tune from history, or use a [burn rate alert](node:Burn%20rate%20alert) |
| Flapping            | Fires and clears every few minutes  | Longer window, separate clear threshold   |
| Duplicates          | One outage sends 200 pages          | Group and deduplicate                     |
| Stale               | Nobody knows why it exists          | Review and delete                         |
| Expected            | Deployment restarts trigger a page  | Silence during known changes              |

Review alerts as a routine. At the end of each on-call shift, go through every page and ask three questions: was it real, did it need a human, and was the action clear? Track the share of pages that needed action. If a hypothetical shift had 40 pages and 6 needed action, precision was 15%, and the other 34 pages are the list to work through.

Repeated interruptions also disrupt sleep and can drive experienced engineers to leave the team.

Teams often hesitate to delete alerts in case one turns out to matter. Moving to [symptom-based alerting](node:Symptom-based%20alerting) reduces that risk, because user impact is covered whatever the cause. If you are unsure about a specific alert, demote it to a ticket for a month and see whether anyone misses it.
quotes: I muted the channel, it's just the same five alerts all day.
That's alert fatigue, and it's how we missed the payment page last week. Let's review every alert from this rota on Friday.

nodes.name: Symptom-based alerting
nodes.description: Paging on what users experience, such as errors and slowness, instead of on internal causes such as high CPU.
nodes.markdown:
Symptom-based alerting is paging on what users experience, such as failed or slow requests, instead of on internal conditions that may or may not matter. A symptom is what is wrong from the user's side. A cause is why it is happening.

| Aspect                     | Cause-based [alert](node:Alert) | Symptom-based alert              |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Example                    | CPU above 90%                   | Checkout errors threatening the [SLO](node:SLO) |
| Fires with no user harm    | Often                           | Rarely                           |
| Catches unforeseen failures | Only the listed causes         | Any cause with visible impact    |
| Explains why               | Sometimes                       | No, this needs investigation     |

Cause-based alerts fail in two directions. One replica dies behind a load balancer, traffic moves to the others, no user notices, and someone is still woken at 3am. On another night a bad configuration fails every payment while CPU, memory and disk stay normal, and nothing pages. Teams recognise this as being woken for harmless events and missing the serious ones.

To implement it, measure an [SLI](node:SLI) close to the user and alert on it, commonly with a [burn rate alert](node:Burn%20rate%20alert). Keep cause data on dashboards, such as the [golden signals](node:Golden%20signals), where it helps with diagnosis once a page has fired.

Some causes still warrant an alert, because by the time the symptom appears it is too late to act cheaply. A disk filling up, a certificate about to expire, a quota nearly reached and a failing backup job all belong here. These alerts give lead time, and many can be tickets.

Low-traffic services need extra care, because one failure in ten requests reads as a 10% error rate. Add a minimum request count to the rule, or use [synthetic monitoring](node:Synthetic%20monitoring) to provide steady traffic. For data pipelines, the symptom is usually stale data, so alert on freshness.
quotes: Should we page when a Kafka broker goes down?
Not by itself. With symptom-based alerting we page if producers start failing, and a lost broker opens a ticket for the morning.

nodes.name: Burn rate alert
nodes.description: An alert on how fast an error budget is being spent, so severe failures page quickly and slow ones raise a ticket.
nodes.markdown:
A burn rate [alert](node:Alert) fires based on how fast a service is consuming its [error budget](node:Error%20budget). Burn rate is the observed error rate divided by the error rate the [SLO](node:SLO) allows. A burn rate of 1 spends the budget exactly over the SLO window, and a burn rate of 10 spends it in a tenth of the window.

For a 99.9% SLO over 30 days, the allowed error rate is 0.1%. An observed error rate of 1.44% is a burn rate of 14.4, and at that pace the 720-hour budget lasts 50 hours.

Plain thresholds handle this badly. A rule such as "errors above 0.1% for 5 minutes" pages on small blips that cost almost no budget, while a steady leak just under the threshold never fires.

The Google SRE Workbook recommends pairing a long and a short window at several burn rates:

| Severity | Long window | Short window | Burn rate | Budget spent | Error rate at 99.9% |
| -------- | ----------- | ------------ | --------- | ------------ | ------------------- |
| Page     | 1 hour      | 5 minutes    | 14.4      | 2%           | 1.44%               |
| Page     | 6 hours     | 30 minutes   | 6         | 5%           | 0.6%                |
| Ticket   | 3 days      | 6 hours      | 1         | 10%          | 0.1%                |

Budget spent is burn rate x long window / 720 hours, so the first row is 14.4 x 1 / 720 = 2%.

Both windows must exceed the threshold. The long window shows that a meaningful amount of budget has gone. The short window, one twelfth of the long one, confirms the problem is still happening, so the alert clears soon after a fix.

Low-traffic services need adjustment, since one failure in 50 requests is a 2% error rate. Add a minimum request count or synthetic traffic.
quotes: Error rate is only 0.7%. Is that worth waking anyone?
On a 99.9% SLO that's a burn rate of 7, so the budget is gone in about four days. If it holds, the six-hour burn rate alert will page.

nodes.name: On-call
nodes.description: A rota in which an engineer is responsible for responding to production alerts within an agreed time.
nodes.markdown:
On-call is an arrangement in which an engineer is responsible, for a set period, for responding to production [alerts](node:Alert) within an agreed time. Teams share the duty through a rota, commonly changing weekly or daily.

A typical setup has several layers:

| Role               | Responsibility                                          |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Primary            | Receives the page, acknowledges it and starts the response |
| Secondary          | Takes the page if the primary does not acknowledge in time |
| Escalation contact | A manager or subject expert for decisions and extra help |

Acknowledging a page means "I have this". If nobody acknowledges within a set time, often 5 to 15 minutes, the paging tool escalates to the next layer. Required response times usually depend on the [severity level](node:Severity%20level).

Rota size determines how sustainable the duty is. With six people on a weekly rota, each engineer is on-call one week in six. Teams spread across time zones can use a follow-the-sun rota, where each region covers its own daytime so nobody is paged overnight.

An unhealthy rota is easy to recognise. People dread their week, sleep badly, and one person gets called regardless of who is on duty because only they understand a particular system. The usual causes are noisy alerts that produce [alert fatigue](node:Alert%20fatigue), knowledge held by one person, and a missing [runbook](node:Runbook). Track pages per shift, night-time pages and hours spent, and treat a bad trend as a production problem.

Some practices help. Write handoff notes at the end of each shift covering open issues. Let new engineers shadow a shift before taking one alone. Compensate on-call with pay or time off, including recovery time after a bad night. Quiet shifts can go toward reducing [toil](node:Toil).
quotes: Priya got paged about the billing job again and she's not even on-call this week.
Because she's the only one who knows it. Let's write the runbook and have someone else shadow her next time.

nodes.name: Runbook
nodes.description: A written procedure for diagnosing and handling a specific alert or operational task.
nodes.markdown:
A runbook is a written procedure for diagnosing and handling a specific [alert](node:Alert) or operational task. Its reader is an [on-call](node:On-call) engineer who may not know the service and may have just been woken up.

A typical runbook follows this order:

| Section         | Contents                                                     |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| What this means | The alert in plain language, and the likely user impact      |
| Check           | Dashboards, queries and commands that confirm the problem    |
| Mitigate        | Ordered, safe actions with exact commands                    |
| Verify          | What recovery looks like                                     |
| Escalate        | Who to contact and when                                      |
| Context         | Links to architecture notes and past [incidents](node:Incident) |

The problem a runbook solves shows up at 3am. A page says "queue depth high" with no link. The wiki page someone finds is two years old and refers to a host that no longer exists, so the responder ends up phoning a colleague who is asleep. Linking the runbook directly from the alert removes the search.

Write for someone under pressure. Give exact commands with placeholders, the expected output of each step, and warnings on anything dangerous. Put [mitigation](node:Mitigation) ahead of root-cause analysis, because the first goal is to restore service.

A stale runbook can do harm, since a responder will follow its instructions against a system that has since changed. Keep runbooks near the code, review them when the service changes, and update them after each use. A [game day](node:Game%20day) is a good way to find out whether one still works.

If a runbook is a fixed sequence that needs no judgement, it is [toil](node:Toil) and a candidate for automation, either as a script a person triggers or as a fix that removes the page altogether.
quotes: The alert fired but I have no idea what this consumer even does.
Follow the runbook link in the page. Step two tells you how to drain the queue safely, and it lists who to call if that fails.

nodes.name: Incident
nodes.description: An unplanned disruption or degradation of a service that needs a coordinated response to restore normal operation.
nodes.markdown:
An incident is an unplanned disruption or degradation of a service that requires a coordinated response. A server crash absorbed by redundancy is a normal event. The same crash causing failed user requests is an incident. Many teams also declare incidents for security events and serious near misses.

An incident generally moves through these stages:

| Step    | Who                       | What happens                                                        |
| ------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Detect  | [Alert](node:Alert) or customer | The problem is noticed                                        |
| Triage  | [On-call](node:On-call) engineer | Assesses impact and sets a [severity level](node:Severity%20level) |
| Declare | On-call engineer          | Opens a channel and names an [incident commander](node:Incident%20commander) |
| Mitigate | Responders               | Applies a [mitigation](node:Mitigation) to restore service          |
| Resolve | Responders                | Confirms recovery and closes the incident                           |
| Learn   | Team                      | Writes a [blameless postmortem](node:Blameless%20postmortem)        |

The cost of having no process is easy to recognise. Five engineers debug separately in direct messages, two of them push different changes at the same moment, support has no idea what to tell customers, and nobody knows who is in charge. Declaring an incident creates one place to talk and clear roles.

Declare early. A false alarm costs a few minutes to close, while a late declaration leaves people working without coordination during the period that matters. Written criteria remove the need for judgement under stress, for example any customer-visible impact lasting over 10 minutes, any risk to data, or any problem needing more than one team.

During the response, keep a timestamped record of observations and actions, since memory of the sequence fades quickly and the review depends on it. Send stakeholders updates at a regular interval, even when the update is that nothing has changed.

Each incident spends [error budget](node:Error%20budget), and its timings feed measures such as [MTTD](node:MTTD) and [MTTR](node:MTTR).
quotes: Should I open an incident? It might just be a blip on the payments graph.
Open it. If it's nothing, we close it in five minutes, and if it's real we already have a channel and a commander.

nodes.name: Severity level
nodes.description: A ranking of an incident's impact that sets how urgently people respond and who gets involved.
nodes.markdown:
A severity level is a ranking of an [incident](node:Incident)'s impact that determines how urgently people respond and who gets involved. Most organisations use labels such as SEV1 to SEV4 or P0 to P3, with lower numbers meaning more serious. Exact definitions vary between companies.

Here is an example scale:

| Level | Impact                                        | Response                                  | Example                       |
| ----- | --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| SEV1  | Critical service down, or data at risk        | Page now, [incident commander](node:Incident%20commander), executive updates | Checkout down for all users |
| SEV2  | Major degradation, or key feature down for some | Page now, incident commander            | Search failing in one region  |
| SEV3  | Minor or partial impact with a workaround     | Handle in working hours                   | Report exports running slow   |
| SEV4  | Cosmetic or no user impact                    | Ticket                                    | Broken chart on an admin page |

Define levels by user impact, and not by the technical cause or by who is complaining. Measurable criteria help: share of users affected, revenue at risk, data loss, security exposure. Without them, the familiar result is an argument in the incident channel about whether this is a SEV1 or a SEV2 while nobody works on the fix. Scales also decay in two directions. If everything is labelled SEV1, the label stops producing urgency. If teams label things low to avoid scrutiny, serious problems miss review.

When unsure, choose the higher level and downgrade later. Severity is expected to change as responders learn more, and each change should be recorded in the timeline.

Severity should drive process automatically. For example, SEV1 and SEV2 might require a [blameless postmortem](node:Blameless%20postmortem), a status page update and customer notification.

Avoid using severity counts as a performance target for teams. Judging a team on its number of SEV1s encourages under-reporting, and hidden incidents cannot be learned from.
quotes: Is this a SEV1? Only the EU region is affected.
EU is 40% of our customers and they can't pay. By our criteria that's a SEV1, and we can downgrade if the impact narrows.

nodes.name: Incident commander
nodes.description: The person who coordinates an incident response, assigning roles and making decisions instead of debugging.
nodes.markdown:
An [incident](node:Incident) commander (IC) is the person who coordinates the response: assigning work, tracking progress, making decisions and keeping communication flowing. The IC does not debug. The role is adapted from the Incident Command System, which US emergency services developed in the 1970s to coordinate wildfire response.

The role exists because of what happens without it. The most senior engineer starts debugging and becomes absorbed. Nobody updates support, and two people apply conflicting fixes. Someone reading a stack trace cannot also track five workstreams.

Larger incidents split the work into roles:

| Role                | Responsibility                                  |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Incident commander  | Owns the overall response and decisions         |
| Operations lead     | Directs technical investigation and changes     |
| Communications lead | Updates stakeholders and customers              |
| Scribe              | Records the timeline, findings and decisions    |

In a small incident, one person may hold several of these roles. If the IC needs to go deep on a technical problem, they should hand over command first.

The IC runs a repeating loop: what do we know, what are we trying, who owns it, and when do we check back? Each action gets a named owner and a time, as in "Sam, roll back payments and report in five minutes". The IC keeps the group focused on [mitigation](node:Mitigation) over root-cause analysis while users are affected.

The IC does not need to be the most senior person or the deepest expert on the system. The job calls for coordination skills, and authority during the incident comes from the role.

Handovers should be explicit and announced in the channel. In long incidents, rotate the IC every few hours to avoid exhausted decisions. Teams can build this skill by shadowing and during a [game day](node:Game%20day).
quotes: Everyone's in the call and three people are suggesting different fixes.
We need an incident commander. I'll take it. Dana, you own the rollback, and everyone else hold changes until she reports back.

nodes.name: Mitigation
nodes.description: An action that reduces or stops user impact during an incident, even if the underlying fault is not yet fixed.
nodes.markdown:
Mitigation is an action that reduces or stops user impact during an [incident](node:Incident), even while the underlying fault is still present. A rollback that restores service without explaining the bug is a mitigation. The permanent fix comes afterwards.

Responders usually choose from a familiar set of options:

| Mitigation           | Use when                              | Watch for                                 |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Roll back            | A recent release lines up with onset  | Schema or data changes may not reverse    |
| Disable a feature flag, a switch that turns code off without a deploy | A new feature is at fault | Other code may depend on it |
| Drain or fail over   | One host, zone or region is bad       | The rest must absorb the traffic          |
| Shed load            | Demand exceeds capacity               | Some users get errors by design           |
| Restart              | A process is stuck or leaking         | Destroys evidence, and the fault may recur |

The common failure is spending 90 minutes establishing the root cause while users stay down, when a rollback was available in the first ten. Stop the impact first and explain it later. If an incident began right after a change, reversing that change is usually the first thing to try.

Capture evidence where it is cheap. A heap dump, thread dump or saved [log](node:Log) excerpt taken before a restart may be the only record of the faulty state. Do not hold up recovery to collect it.

Apply one change at a time where possible, so you can tell what worked, and confirm the effect using a user-level [SLI](node:SLI) instead of assuming.

A mitigation also needs a follow-up. Temporary measures such as extra replicas or a disabled job tend to become permanent unless someone tracks them. The time taken to reach this point is what the "restore" version of [MTTR](node:MTTR) measures.
quotes: I think I've nearly found the bug, give me another twenty minutes.
Users are still down. Roll back as the mitigation now, then keep digging with the pressure off.

nodes.name: Blameless postmortem
nodes.description: A written review of an incident that examines how the system allowed it, without assigning fault to individuals.
nodes.markdown:
A blameless postmortem is a written review of an [incident](node:Incident) that examines how the system and organisation allowed it to happen, without assigning fault to individuals. It starts from the assumption that people acted reasonably given what they knew at the time.

The reason is practical. If admitting a mistake leads to punishment, people stop reporting mistakes and leave details out, and the organisation loses the information it needs. The recognisable failure is a report concluding "engineer ran the wrong command, reminded to be more careful". Nothing changes, and the same failure returns. Better questions are why one command could do that much damage, why nothing asked for confirmation, and why staging behaved differently.

A typical document contains:

| Section                                             | Contents                                         |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Summary                                             | What happened, in a few sentences                |
| Impact                                              | Users affected, duration, [error budget](node:Error%20budget) spent |
| Timeline                                            | Timestamped events and decisions                 |
| [Contributing factors](node:Contributing%20factor)  | Conditions that allowed or worsened the failure  |
| What went well                                      | Practices worth keeping                          |
| Action items                                        | Specific changes, each with an owner and due date |

Blameless does not mean unaccountable. People are still expected to take part honestly and to complete their actions. Many teams refer to roles in the document, such as "the [on-call](node:On-call) engineer", instead of names.

Action items are where postmortems most often fail. Vague, unowned items such as "improve [monitoring](node:Monitoring)" are forgotten once the document is filed. Write specific, checkable items, such as "page when payment errors burn budget at 14.4 times the allowed rate". Prefer changes to systems over training or reminders, because systems do not depend on someone remembering. Track items to completion with the same priority as feature work.

Hold the review within a few days and share the result widely.
quotes: The postmortem draft says Tom caused the outage by deploying on Friday.
Rewrite that. Ask why our pipeline let a broken config reach every region, because that's still true whoever deploys next.

nodes.name: Contributing factor
nodes.description: A condition that helped an incident happen or made it worse, used in place of naming one single root cause.
nodes.markdown:
A contributing factor is a condition that helped an [incident](node:Incident) happen or made it worse. Incident reviews use the term because failures in complex systems rarely have one cause. Several ordinary conditions, each harmless alone, combine.

Consider a hypothetical incident in which a configuration change sets a timeout to zero and takes an API down for 50 minutes:

| Contributing factor                       | Effect                            | Action                                              |
| ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Config values were not validated          | The bad value was accepted        | Add schema validation                               |
| Change applied to all regions at once     | Local mistake became global       | Roll out region by region                           |
| [Alerts](node:Alert) watched only CPU     | Detected after 20 minutes, by support | Add [symptom-based alerting](node:Symptom-based%20alerting) |
| [Runbook](node:Runbook) had an old command | Recovery took 15 minutes longer  | Update and test it                                  |

A trigger is different from a factor. The trigger is the event that set off the failure, here the config change. The factors explain why that event did so much damage, and most of them existed long before the day of the incident.

Asking for a single root cause tends to stop the investigation at the first plausible answer, which is often the last human action: "an engineer pushed bad config". Fixing only that leaves every other condition in place, ready to combine with the next mistake. The symptom is a team that closes each incident with a fix and still sees the same kind of failure return with a different trigger.

"Human error" is not a useful factor on its own. Treat it as the start of the question: what made this action easy to get wrong and hard to notice?

Not every factor deserves work. In a [blameless postmortem](node:Blameless%20postmortem), record a decision for each one: fix it, monitor it or accept the risk explicitly.
quotes: Can we just put 'bad deploy' as the root cause and close this?
The deploy was the trigger. No canary and a silent alert were contributing factors, and those will bite us again.

nodes.name: Capacity planning
nodes.description: Forecasting future demand and arranging enough resources to serve it while still meeting reliability targets.
nodes.markdown:
Capacity planning is forecasting future demand and arranging enough resources to serve it while still meeting [SLOs](node:SLO). It covers compute, storage, network, database connections and third-party quotas.

The process follows a repeating sequence, shown here with hypothetical numbers:

| Step | Action                    | Example                                      |
| ---- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Measure current peak      | 6,000 requests per second                    |
| 2    | Forecast growth           | 10% a month for 6 months gives about 10,630  |
| 3    | Measure unit capacity     | [Load testing](node:Load%20testing) shows 500 per instance within SLO |
| 4    | Calculate need            | 10,630 / 500 = 21.26, so 22 instances        |
| 5    | Add redundancy            | To survive losing one of 3 zones, 11 per zone, 33 total |
| 6    | Review                    | Compare forecast with actual each quarter    |

Step 5 is often skipped. With 22 instances spread over three zones, losing a zone leaves 14 or 15, which cannot carry the forecast peak. With 33, the remaining two zones hold 22.

Forecasts need two inputs. Organic growth is the steady trend visible in historical data. Inorganic growth comes from launches, marketing campaigns and large new customers, and it appears in no graph until it happens. The familiar failure is a launch that takes the site down because nobody told the infrastructure team about it.

Lead times shape the plan. Quota increases, hardware orders and splitting a database can take weeks. Autoscaling, which adds instances automatically as load rises, does not remove the need to plan. It reacts with a delay, stops at quota limits and does not help components that cannot scale out, such as a single primary database.

Plan around [saturation](node:Saturation) instead of CPU alone, and keep headroom, because [queueing delay](node:Queueing%20delay) rises sharply near capacity. Re-measure unit capacity after major releases, since a performance regression changes every number above.
quotes: Marketing is running a TV ad in March. Do we need to do anything?
Yes, get the expected traffic from them now. Capacity planning needs a number, and our database quota takes weeks to raise.

nodes.name: Load testing
nodes.description: Sending realistic traffic to a system at expected volumes to check that it meets its performance targets.
nodes.markdown:
Load testing is sending realistic traffic to a system at expected volumes to check whether it meets its performance targets. A typical question is whether the service can handle next month's peak with p99 latency under 300 ms.

It belongs to a family of tests that ask different questions:

| Test                                | Question                          | Load shape                 | Typical duration   |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
| Load test                           | Does it meet targets at expected load? | Ramp to peak and hold | Minutes to an hour |
| [Stress test](node:Stress%20testing) | Where and how does it break?     | Increase past capacity     | Until failure      |
| [Soak test](node:Soak%20test)       | Does it degrade over time?        | Steady and moderate        | Hours to days      |

The result is only as good as the realism of the test. The common symptom is a system that passes at 5,000 requests per second and falls over in production at 2,000. Usual reasons are simulated users all requesting the same cached URL, a test database far smaller than production, missing background jobs, and an environment that differs from production.

Derive the traffic mix from production [logs](node:Log). Use data volumes close to production. Ramp up gradually and hold long enough to get past cold caches. Report [percentiles](node:Percentile) and error rates, not averages.

Watch the load generator too. If it runs out of CPU, the latencies it reports are wrong. Prefer an open workload, which sends requests at a fixed arrival rate whatever the responses do. Tools that wait for each reply slow down along with the server and hide the delay, an error called [coordinated omission](node:Coordinated%20omission).

[Little's Law](node:Little's%20Law) gives a quick sanity check: 50 clients that each wait for a reply at 200 ms average latency cannot exceed 250 requests per second.

Results feed directly into [capacity planning](node:Capacity%20planning).
quotes: The load test passed at twice our peak, so Black Friday is safe.
It also hit one product page with an empty cart table. Replay real traffic against a production-sized database before we trust that.

nodes.name: Stress testing
nodes.description: Pushing a system past its expected capacity to find where it breaks, how it fails and whether it recovers.
nodes.markdown:
Stress testing is pushing a system beyond its expected capacity to find where it breaks, how it fails and whether it recovers. [Load testing](node:Load%20testing) asks whether a system meets its targets at expected demand.

A stress test usually runs in phases:

| Phase    | Action                               | Record                                   |
| -------- | ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| Baseline | Run at normal load                   | Latency and error rate                   |
| Ramp     | Raise load in steps, holding each    | The point where the [SLO](node:SLO) fails |
| Break    | Continue until errors dominate       | First resource to reach [saturation](node:Saturation) |
| Recover  | Drop back to normal load             | Time to recover, or failure to recover   |

The first useful output is the knee: the load at which latency starts rising sharply because [queueing delay](node:Queueing%20delay) takes over. Plan capacity below the knee, not at the point of collapse.

How the system fails matters as much as where. In a graceful failure, it rejects excess requests quickly and keeps serving what it can. In a collapse, it accepts everything, queues grow, timeouts trigger retries, and it spends its time on requests whose clients have already given up. Throughput then falls as load rises.

The recovery phase catches a difficult case known as a metastable failure, where the system stays broken after the original trigger has gone. Retries or cold caches keep load above what it can handle. In production this appears as a traffic spike that has passed while the service stays down until someone restarts it or blocks traffic. A [thundering herd](node:Thundering%20herd) is a frequent cause.

Findings usually lead to load shedding (rejecting excess work on purpose), bounded queues, timeouts, and retry budgets that cap retries as a share of requests.

Run stress tests in an isolated environment, and confirm that each [alert](node:Alert) fires at the expected point.
quotes: We know it handles 8,000 requests a second. What happens at 12,000?
Nobody knows. Let's stress test it in staging, then drop the load and see if it recovers without a restart.

nodes.name: Soak test
nodes.description: Running a system at steady, realistic load for hours or days to expose problems that only appear over time.
nodes.markdown:
A soak test runs a system at steady, realistic load for an extended period, typically hours or days, to expose problems that only appear over time. It is also called an endurance test. A short [load test](node:Load%20testing) can pass while the system is slowly heading toward failure.

Soak tests find a specific class of defect:

| Problem                         | What you see over time                         |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| [Memory leak](node:Memory%20leak) | Memory floor climbs until the process is killed |
| Connection leak                 | Open connections rise until the pool runs out  |
| Disk growth                     | [Logs](node:Log) or temp files fill the disk   |
| Data growth                     | Queries slow down as tables grow               |
| Time-based events               | Token expiry, scheduled jobs, log rotation     |

The recognisable symptom is a service that runs well after each deployment and dies after a few days. Teams that deploy often may never see the problem, because each release restarts the process and resets the clock. It then surfaces during a holiday change freeze, when the service runs uninterrupted for longer than it ever has.

Run the test at roughly typical production load. Make it longer than the longest cycle you care about. If a batch job runs daily or an access token lasts 24 hours, a soak of under a day will not exercise them.

Watch the trend instead of the level. Graph each [gauge](node:Gauge) for memory, connections, threads and disk, and compare the first hour with the last. A flat line is healthy, and a slope gives a time to failure. In a hypothetical test where memory grows 20 MB per hour with 1.6 GB free, the process runs out after 80 hours. An 8-hour soak would not crash, but its slope reveals the problem.
quotes: It passed the load test, but in production it falls over every four days.
An hour-long test can't catch that. Run a soak test over the weekend and watch the memory and connection graphs.

nodes.name: Little's Law
nodes.description: A queueing rule. The average number of items in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each item spends there.
nodes.markdown:
Little's Law states that the average number of items in a stable system equals the average arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends in the system. John Little published a proof in 1961.

```text
L = λ × W
```

L is the average number in the system, λ (lambda) is the arrival rate, and W is the average time in the system. The units must match, so convert milliseconds to seconds when the rate is per second. The law holds whatever the arrival pattern or distribution of service times, as long as the system is stable over the period measured.

It answers common sizing questions, shown here with hypothetical numbers:

| Question                                         | Calculation | Answer             |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ----------- | ------------------ |
| Requests in flight at 200 per second and 250 ms? | 200 x 0.25  | 50 concurrent      |
| Maximum rate for 100 connections held 50 ms each? | 100 / 0.05 | 2,000 per second   |

The law explains a confusing kind of outage, where a slow dependency exhausts threads in a service that has no bug. At 200 requests per second and 250 ms, a service holds 50 requests in flight. If a dependency slows and requests now take one second, the same traffic needs 200 in flight. With a pool of 100 threads, requests begin to queue or fail although traffic never changed.

The law describes averages, so it says nothing about [percentiles](node:Percentile) or short bursts, and sizing needs headroom on top. It does not apply while arrivals exceed completions, because the queue keeps growing and no steady average exists. Related limits appear as [saturation](node:Saturation) and [queueing delay](node:Queueing%20delay).
quotes: How big should the connection pool be for the new service?
Little's Law says 500 queries a second at 20 ms is 10 in flight on average. Start around 20 for bursts and watch wait time.

nodes.name: Queueing delay
nodes.description: Time a request spends waiting for a busy resource before work on it starts. It grows sharply near full utilisation.
nodes.markdown:
Queueing delay is the time a request spends waiting for a busy resource before any work on it begins. Total latency is queueing delay plus service time, the time spent doing the work.

A simple queueing model, known as M/M/1, assumes one server, random arrivals and exponentially distributed service times. In this model the average total time is S / (1 - U), where S is service time and U is utilisation. With a 10 ms service time:

| Utilisation | Average wait | Average total |
| ----------- | ------------ | ------------- |
| 50%         | 10 ms        | 20 ms         |
| 80%         | 40 ms        | 50 ms         |
| 90%         | 90 ms        | 100 ms        |
| 95%         | 190 ms       | 200 ms        |
| 99%         | 990 ms       | 1,000 ms      |

Moving from 90% to 99% utilisation is 10% more traffic and ten times the latency. Real systems have different numbers, since multiple workers soften the curve and bursty traffic worsens it, but the shape holds.

The symptom is a service that is fine all day until a small rise at peak makes latency jump. Engineers search for a bad query or a recent deployment that does not exist. Each request takes no longer to process once it starts, so [profiling](node:Profiling) shows nothing new. In a [distributed trace](node:Distributed%20trace), the time appears as a gap before a [span](node:Span) begins or between client and server spans.

To respond, keep utilisation below the steep part of the curve through [capacity planning](node:Capacity%20planning), reduce service time or add workers. Bound queues and reject work when they fill, because a request served after its client has given up is wasted. Track queue depth or wait time as a [saturation](node:Saturation) signal. [Little's Law](node:Little's%20Law) connects the two: 30 requests waiting at 200 per second means a 150 ms average wait.
quotes: Traffic is up 8% and p99 tripled. Did someone ship something?
Nothing shipped. We're at 92% utilisation, so that's queueing delay. Add two instances and it should drop.

nodes.name: Coordinated omission
nodes.description: A load-testing error where the tool sends fewer requests during a stall, so the slowest latencies go unrecorded.
nodes.markdown:
Coordinated omission is a measurement error in which a load generator slows down when the system under test slows down, and so never records the latency of requests it should have sent. Gil Tene gave the problem its name. It makes [tail latency](node:Tail%20latency) look far better than it is.

The mechanism is a closed loop. Many tools wait for each response before sending the next request. During a stall, the tool sends nothing, so the tool and the server in effect cooperate to leave out samples at the moment the measurements would be worst.

Take a hypothetical test intended to send 100 requests per second for 60 seconds over one connection. Responses normally take 5 ms, and the server stalls once for 10 seconds.

| Measure                   | Recorded by closed-loop tool | Measured from intended send times |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Requests counted          | 5,001                        | 6,000                             |
| Requests delayed by stall | 1                            | 1,000                             |
| [p99](node:Percentile)    | 5 ms                         | About 9.4 s                       |
| Maximum                   | 10 s                         | 10 s                              |

The 1,000 requests scheduled during the stall would have waited between nearly 0 and 10 seconds. The tool saw only one of them.

The symptom is a [load test](node:Load%20testing) reporting a p99 of a few milliseconds while users see multi-second pauses in production. A high maximum next to a low p99 is a warning sign.

To avoid it, use an open-loop generator that launches requests on a fixed schedule regardless of outstanding responses, and measure latency from the intended start time.

Production measurement can have the same blind spot. A service that starts its timer when a handler begins does not count [queueing delay](node:Queueing%20delay) before that point. Measure at the client or load balancer as well.
quotes: The benchmark says p99 is 4 ms, but we saw a ten-second GC pause during the run.
Then it's coordinated omission. The tool stopped sending during the pause, so rerun it with a constant arrival rate.

nodes.name: Thundering herd
nodes.description: Many clients acting at the same moment, such as after a cache expiry or outage, and overwhelming a shared resource.
nodes.markdown:
A thundering herd is many clients or processes acting at the same moment and overwhelming a shared resource. Something usually synchronises them: a cache expiry, a service restart, a scheduled job or a reconnect after a failure.

| Trigger                      | What happens                            | Countermeasure                                     |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Popular cache key expires    | Every request hits the database at once | Request coalescing, where one fetches and others wait |
| Many keys share one lifetime | They all expire together                | Add a random offset to each expiry                 |
| Service recovers from outage | All clients reconnect and retry         | Exponential backoff with jitter                    |
| Midnight scheduled job       | The whole fleet runs it simultaneously  | Randomise start times                              |
| Cold restart                 | Empty caches send all reads downstream  | Warm caches and ramp traffic gradually             |

The recognisable symptom is a service that comes back after an outage and immediately falls over again. Engineers restart it, it survives for seconds, and the cycle repeats. Load at recovery can exceed the normal peak, because clients have accumulated retries and every one of them tries at once.

Randomness breaks the synchronisation. If 1,000 clients each retry after exactly 5 seconds, the server receives 1,000 requests in the same instant, round after round. Spreading those retries randomly over 30 seconds gives about 33 per second. This random spread is called jitter. Exponential backoff, which lengthens the wait after each failure, is not enough alone, because clients that failed together still retry together at 1, 2 and 4 seconds.

During recovery, the usual [mitigation](node:Mitigation) is to admit traffic in stages at the load balancer and reject the excess until caches are warm. The recovery phase of [stress testing](node:Stress%20testing) can expose this behaviour in advance.
quotes: We brought the API back and it died again in thirty seconds.
That's a thundering herd, every mobile client is retrying at once. Let traffic in 10% at a time and add jitter to the client backoff.

nodes.name: Memory leak
nodes.description: Memory a program keeps allocated after it stops needing it, so usage climbs until the process slows or is killed.
nodes.markdown:
A memory leak is memory that a program keeps allocated after it no longer needs it, so usage climbs until the process slows down or is killed. In manually managed languages such as C, it is memory that was never freed. In garbage-collected languages, the collector cannot release anything still referenced, so a leak is usually an object kept reachable by accident. Common causes are unbounded caches, global maps keyed by request or user, event listeners never removed, and threads blocked forever while holding references.

The usual symptom is that a restart fixes everything for a while. The memory [gauge](node:Gauge) climbs steadily, the process is killed for exceeding its limit, it restarts, and the cycle repeats at a regular interval.

The shape of the memory graph helps separate a leak from normal behaviour:

| Pattern                         | Likely meaning                                |
| ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Sawtooth with a flat floor      | Normal garbage collection                     |
| Sawtooth with a rising floor    | Leak                                          |
| Rises, then plateaus            | A cache filling to its limit                  |
| Sudden step with a traffic burst | Large allocation, not necessarily a leak     |
| Process memory grows, heap flat | Native memory use or fragmentation            |

Small leaks add up under traffic. If each request retains 2 KB at a hypothetical 100 requests per second, the process leaks 200 KB per second, or 720 MB per hour. A container with a 2 GB limit and a 500 MB baseline has 1.5 GB of headroom and would be killed after about two hours.

To diagnose a leak, take two heap snapshots some time apart under load, compare which object types grew, and find what is holding references to them. Heap [profiling](node:Profiling) supports this directly. A [soak test](node:Soak%20test) can reproduce the problem before release, whereas frequent deployments can hide it by restarting the process.
quotes: The worker gets OOM-killed every six hours, like clockwork.
Sounds like a memory leak. Grab two heap dumps an hour apart and diff them to see what's growing.

nodes.name: Profiling
nodes.description: Measuring where a running program spends CPU, memory or waiting time, down to individual functions.
nodes.markdown:
Profiling is measuring where a running program spends resources, such as CPU time, memory or waiting time, down to the level of individual functions. It replaces guesses about performance with data. The familiar failure it prevents is spending two days optimising a function that turns out to account for 1% of runtime, where even a perfect fix could save at most 1%.

Different profile types answer different questions:

| Type       | Question                      | Useful when                           |
| ---------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| CPU        | Which code is on the CPU?     | High CPU or slow computation          |
| Heap       | What is holding memory now?   | Investigating a [memory leak](node:Memory%20leak) |
| Allocation | What allocates the most?      | Heavy garbage collection              |
| Off-CPU    | Where are threads blocked?    | Slow service with low CPU             |

Profilers work in two main ways. A [sampling](node:Sampling) profiler interrupts the program at a fixed frequency, such as 99 times per second, and records the call stack. Its overhead is low, and functions that use a lot of time appear in many samples. An instrumenting profiler records every function entry and exit, which is exact but slower and can distort the behaviour being measured. Sampling is the usual choice in production.

A CPU profile does not show waiting. A request that uses 10 ms of CPU and blocks for 900 ms on a database barely appears in it, which is why a slow service can produce a CPU profile with nothing interesting in it. Use an off-CPU profile or a [distributed trace](node:Distributed%20trace) for that case.

Continuous profiling runs low-overhead sampling across production all the time. It lets you compare before and after a deployment, or inspect the moment of an [incident](node:Incident) without reproducing it. Results are commonly displayed as a [flame graph](node:Flame%20graph).
quotes: I'm going to rewrite the JSON parser, it has to be what's slow.
Profile it first. Last time we guessed, the parser was 2% of CPU and the real cost was in logging.

nodes.name: Flame graph
nodes.description: A chart of profiled call stacks where each box's width shows its share of samples, used to find expensive code.
nodes.markdown:
A flame graph is a visualisation of [profiling](node:Profiling) data that shows sampled call stacks, with each box's width proportional to the share of samples in which that function appeared. Brendan Gregg created the format.

| Element             | Meaning                                                  |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Box                 | One function in the call stack                           |
| Width               | Share of samples containing this function and its callees |
| Vertical position   | Stack depth, with each callee drawn above its caller     |
| Left-to-right order | Usually alphabetical, and not related to time            |
| Colour              | Usually only separates boxes visually                    |

The common misreading is to treat the horizontal axis as time. Two boxes side by side did not necessarily run one after the other. A view that does plot time horizontally is called a flame chart, as seen in browser developer tools, and it answers a different question.

Look for wide boxes with little or nothing above them. Those functions were themselves on the CPU for that share of samples. A wide box covered by children spent its time in those children. New readers often see the broad `main` or `handleRequest` box at the bottom and conclude it is the problem, when it is only the caller of everything above it.

Width converts to a limit on savings. If `serialize` covers 35% of the graph, making it twice as fast saves at most about 17.5% of CPU.

Differential flame graphs compare two profiles, such as before and after a deployment, and colour the functions that grew or shrank. They are a direct way to investigate a performance regression.

A CPU flame graph shows only on-CPU work, so a service blocked on a database looks idle in it. An off-CPU variant covers blocking.
quotes: The flame graph shows handleRequest at 95%. So that's our slow function?
No, that's just the root of the stack. Look at the wide plateau near the top, it's regex compilation at 30%.

nodes.name: Chaos engineering
nodes.description: Deliberately injecting failures into a system in a controlled way to test whether it behaves as expected.
nodes.markdown:
Chaos engineering is the practice of deliberately injecting failures into a system, as a controlled experiment, to test whether it behaves as expected. It grew out of work at Netflix, whose Chaos Monkey tool randomly terminated production instances.

The practice is an experiment with a defined method:

| Step | Action                 | Example                                       |
| ---- | ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | Define steady state    | Checkout success stays at or above 99.9%      |
| 2    | Form a hypothesis      | Losing one cache node will not affect checkout |
| 3    | Limit the blast radius | 1% of traffic in one zone                     |
| 4    | Set abort conditions   | Stop if the [SLI](node:SLI) drops below target |
| 5    | Inject the fault       | Terminate a cache node                        |
| 6    | Observe and compare    | Did steady state hold?                        |
| 7    | Fix and repeat         | Address what was learned                      |

The problem it addresses is redundancy that has never been exercised. A team has a standby database and a failover procedure that has never run. On the day the primary fails, the standby turns out to have stale configuration or too little capacity.

Typical injected faults include instance termination, added network latency, packet loss, dependency errors, DNS failures, full disks and clock skew. Added latency is often more revealing than a crash, because a slow dependency ties up threads and connections while a dead one fails quickly.

Some preconditions apply. You need enough [observability](node:Observability) to see the effect, an [SLO](node:SLO) to define normal, and a fast way to stop. If you already expect the system to fail the experiment, fix it first. Start in staging and move to production as confidence grows, since only production has real traffic and configuration.

Experiments that affect users spend [error budget](node:Error%20budget), so run them when budget is available. A [game day](node:Game%20day) complements this work by exercising the people as well as the software.
quotes: We've got three replicas, so losing one is fine.
Have we ever tried it? Let's run a chaos engineering experiment on 1% of traffic and see whether failover works.

nodes.name: Game day
nodes.description: A scheduled exercise in which a team simulates a failure and practises detecting, responding to and recovering from it.
nodes.markdown:
A game day is a scheduled exercise in which a team simulates a failure and practises detecting it, responding to it and recovering from it. [Chaos engineering](node:Chaos%20engineering) tests how software behaves. A game day also tests people, tools and procedures.

An exercise usually runs through these phases:

| Phase   | What happens                                                 |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Plan    | Choose the scenario, scope, participants and abort criteria  |
| Brief   | Tell stakeholders the time and the possible impact           |
| Inject  | A facilitator triggers or simulates the failure              |
| Respond | [On-call](node:On-call) engineers work it as a real [incident](node:Incident) |
| Recover | Restore normal operation and confirm the system is healthy   |
| Debrief | Record the gaps and assign actions                           |

The problem it addresses is discovering a broken procedure during a real outage. The first attempt to restore a database from backup should not be the one that reveals the backup is corrupt or that the restore takes nine hours. Game days also expose missing credentials, an out-of-date [runbook](node:Runbook), an [alert](node:Alert) that never fires, dashboards some responders cannot open, and uncertainty over who may make a decision.

The format can match the team's maturity. A tabletop exercise talks through the scenario without touching any system and costs little. A staging exercise runs real actions safely. A production exercise is the closest to reality and needs strong safeguards.

Keep the exercise realistic. Use the normal tools, practise the [incident commander](node:Incident%20commander) role, and have an observer note where people got stuck. Label all communication as an exercise so nobody mistakes it for a real outage, and stop at once if a real incident begins.

Track the resulting actions as you would those from a [blameless postmortem](node:Blameless%20postmortem). Repeat the exercise periodically, because systems and teams change.
quotes: Our DR plan says we can restore in an hour. Has anyone timed it?
No. Let's schedule a game day next month, restore last night's backup and see how long it takes.

nodes.name: DORA metrics
nodes.description: Measures of software delivery performance from the DORA research programme, covering throughput and instability.
nodes.markdown:
DORA metrics are measures of software delivery performance from the DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) programme. The research originally identified four key metrics. DORA renamed and narrowed one of them in 2023 and added a fifth in 2024.

| Metric                          | Group       | What it measures                                                  |
| ------------------------------- | ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Change lead time                | Throughput  | Time from commit to running in production                         |
| Deployment frequency            | Throughput  | How often deployments happen                                      |
| Failed deployment recovery time | Throughput  | Time to recover from a deployment needing immediate intervention  |
| [Change fail rate](node:Change%20failure%20rate) | Instability | Share of deployments needing immediate intervention |
| Deployment rework rate          | Instability | Share of deployments that are unplanned and caused by a production [incident](node:Incident) |

Failed deployment recovery time replaced "time to restore service". It counts only failures caused by a change, so it excludes events such as a data centre outage, and it is narrower than a general [MTTR](node:MTTR).

DORA's research has found that throughput and stability tend to go together: teams that deploy frequently in small batches generally also have fewer and shorter failures.

The usual misuse is turning these measures into targets or league tables. Once deployment frequency is a goal, teams split releases into trivial deployments. Once failure rate is a goal, failures get reclassified as something else. Comparisons between teams also mislead, since a mobile app that waits on store review and a web service have different constraints. Use the metrics to follow one team's trend and to find its bottleneck.

Agree what counts as a deployment and a failure, and pull the data from the deployment pipeline and incident tracker.

These metrics describe delivery and say nothing directly about user experience. Pair them with an [SLO](node:SLO), since a team can score well on DORA while its service misses its reliability target.
quotes: The VP wants every team ranked on DORA metrics this quarter.
Then we'll get lots of one-line deploys. Let's show each team's own trend and use it to find where changes get stuck.

nodes.name: Change failure rate
nodes.description: The share of deployments that need immediate intervention afterwards, such as a rollback or hotfix.
nodes.markdown:
Change failure rate is the share of deployments to production that need immediate intervention afterwards, such as a rollback or hotfix. It is one of the [DORA metrics](node:DORA%20metrics), where it is named "change fail rate". The formula is failed deployments divided by total deployments. If a team ships 120 deployments in a quarter and 6 need a rollback or hotfix, the rate is 5%.

The number depends on what the team counts as a failure:

| Event                                                  | Usually counts?                |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------ |
| Deployment rolled back because of errors               | Yes                            |
| Hotfix shipped to correct a release                    | Yes                            |
| Caught by a canary, a release sent to a small share of traffic first | Depends, so record the policy |
| Bug found weeks later and fixed in normal work         | No                             |
| Outage caused by a cloud provider                      | No                             |
| Planned rollback for business reasons                  | No                             |

Without agreed definitions, the figure can drift away from reality. The telltale sign is a rate of 1% on a team whose engineers remember constant firefighting. Often failures are being fixed forward in later releases and never labelled as failures. Linking deployments to [incidents](node:Incident) and to hotfix commits gives a more honest count.

The rate says nothing about severity. A change that takes down checkout counts the same as one with a minor effect, so read it alongside [error budget](node:Error%20budget) spend and recovery time.

Deploying less often to reduce failures tends to backfire. Larger batches carry more change per release and are harder to diagnose when they go wrong. To lower the rate, make changes smaller, strengthen automated tests, validate configuration, release to a growing share of traffic, and act on the [contributing factors](node:Contributing%20factor) found in past failures.
quotes: Our change failure rate is 2%, so why does [on-call](node:On-call) feel so bad?
We only count rollbacks. Half our bad releases get patched forward, so let's count those hotfixes too.

nodes.name: Production readiness review
nodes.description: A structured check that a service can be run safely in production before it launches or changes owners.
nodes.markdown:
A production readiness review (PRR) is a structured check that a service can be run safely in production, done before it launches or before another team takes responsibility for it. Google's [site reliability engineering](node:Site%20reliability%20engineering) teams helped popularise the practice.

A review typically covers these areas:

| Area             | Questions                                                                  |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Targets          | Are [SLIs](node:SLI) and [SLOs](node:SLO) defined?                         |
| Visibility       | Is there enough [observability](node:Observability) to debug it?           |
| Alerting         | Does each [alert](node:Alert) reflect user impact and link a [runbook](node:Runbook)? |
| Capacity         | Has [load testing](node:Load%20testing) established its limits?            |
| Failure handling | What happens when each dependency fails?                                   |
| Change safety    | Can a release be rolled back quickly?                                      |
| Data             | Are backups taken, and has a restore been tested?                          |
| Security         | How are secrets and access managed?                                        |
| Ownership        | Who is [on-call](node:On-call), and do they know the service?              |

The problem it prevents is a service that ships on a Friday and pages someone who has never seen it. There are no dashboards, no runbook and no list of dependencies, so the team discovers each gap during its first [incident](node:Incident). A review moves that discovery to a point where fixes are cheaper.

Timing affects the outcome. A review held a week before launch produces a list nobody has time to address, so start the conversation at the design stage. The output should separate blocking items, which must be fixed before launch, from non-blocking items tracked with owners and dates. When a team launches with a known gap, a named person should accept that risk explicitly.

A review can also decay into bureaucracy, where a long generic checklist becomes box-ticking and teams route around it. Scale the rigour to how critical the service is, so an internal tool gets a lighter review than a payment path.
quotes: We're launching the new billing service next Tuesday. Can SRE take the pager?
Not before a production readiness review. Right now it has no runbook, no SLO and an untested restore.
